bib.title: Agents: An Open-source Framework for Autonomous Language Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Agents: An Open-source Framework for Autonomous Language Agents", Wangchunshu Zhou, Yuchen Eleanor Jiang, Long Li, Jialong Wu et al. (AIWaves Inc., Zhejiang Univ., ETH Zurich; 17 authors, Mrinmaya Sachan last). Preprint, arXiv:2309.07870v3 [cs.CL], 12 Dec 2023. The header reads "Preprint. Work in progress." No venue is stated. Library: https://github.com/aiwaves-cn/agents. The note's frontmatter does not list this paper, and the note body does not cite it.

COVERAGE: 10 of 10 pages, 29,997 of 29,997 chars. Pages 1-7 are body, 8-10 are references. There are no appendices and no results tables. The extraction was clean, apart from garbled spacing in the code listings and figure text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The paper is a system description, not an empirical study. It reports no benchmark, ablation, user study, latency or cost figure, and no failure analysis. The only evidence is qualitative case-study screenshots.
  number: none
  setup: Section 4 "Case Studies" covers single-agent systems (chit-chat bot, two customer-service agents, shopping assistant, sales agent) and multi-agent systems (fiction studio, debate, software company). It also has one human-in-the-debate demo. Demos are at aiwaves-agents.com.
  quote: "We then present a few case studies on different language agents built with the library, including single-agent systems, multi-agent systems, and systems that require human-agent interaction."
  where: p.8, Sec 4
- Its only comparative claim is a feature checklist (Table 1). AGENTS is the only one of the nine listed frameworks with all five features ticked. This is self-assessed by the authors, with no criteria given and no pinned versions. Table 1 gives LangChain tool usage and long-short memory but no multi-agent, human-agent or symbolic control. AgentVerse has everything except symbolic control.
  number: none (5 binary columns, 9 frameworks)
  setup: Columns are Tool Usage, Long-short Term Memory, Multi-Agent, Human-Agent Interaction and Symbolic Control. Rows are Transformers Agents, LangChain, Auto-GPT, Gentopia, XLang, Meta-GPT, Camel, AgentVerse and AGENTS.
  quote: "We can see that AGENTS is the only framework that supports tool usage, long-short term memory, and multi-agent communication at the same time. AGENTS also offers human-agent interaction and controllability through symbolic plans (SOPs) for the first time."
  where: p.4, Table 1 and Sec 2.2
- Design claim: control flow can be a symbolic graph of states (an SOP, "standard operating procedure"), where the author writes the states and transitions instead of leaving the LLM to plan freely. The authors say this makes behaviour more stable and predictable and easier to tune. This is asserted and never measured.
  number: none
  setup: An SOP is a graph of State objects. Each State holds PromptComponents (task, rules, demonstrations, output format) and ToolComponents. An LLM-based `sop._transit()` picks the next state and `sop._route()` picks the next agent. SOPs can be LLM-generated and then edited by the user.
  quote: "making agents' behavior more stable/predictable and facilitating tuning/optimizing agents at the same time."
  where: p.3, Sec 1 Controllability; p.5, Sec 3.2
- Motivating claim: frameworks that rely only on a short task description make run-to-run behaviour inconsistent. This is stated without data.
  number: none
  quote: "This results in significant randomness and inconsistency across different runs, delivering an unsatisfactory user experience and making it hard to customize and tune language agents."
  where: p.2, Sec 1
- The core loop is a few lines: the SOP picks the state and agent, the agent acts, the environment updates. The framework has three core classes (Agent, SOP, Environment), all built from a single JSON config. This is useful for the "do you need a framework" comparison, since the whole loop is tiny.
  number: none
  quote: "while not sop . finished :" and "agent , state = sop . step ( agents , e n v i r o n m e n t )"
  where: p.4, Code 2
- Dynamic scheduling: a controller LLM chooses which agent acts next, in place of fixed sequential order. It is configured by a natural-language rule in the config. This is the model-chosen routing that the note's control-flow row contrasts with explicit edges.
  number: none
  quote: "AGENTS includes a controller function that dynamically decides which agent will perform the next action using an LLM by considering the previous actions, the environment, and the target of the current states."
  where: p.6, Sec 3.4
- Memory design: long-term memory is a VectorDB of action histories embedded with sentence-transformers and queried by semantic search. Short-term memory is a natural-language scratchpad rewritten by an LLM. Both are taken from RecurrentGPT (Zhou et al. 2023a).
  number: none
  quote: "long-term memories are action histories and are embedded by sentence-transformers [Reimers and Gurevych, 2019], stored in a VectorDB, and queried via semantic search."
  where: p.6, Sec 3.4
- Human-in-the-loop is a per-agent flag, not a pause or resume mechanism. Setting `_is_human` makes `_act()` show observations to a human and wait for input. This is a human playing an agent role. It is not checkpointing, durable execution or approval gates.
  number: none
  quote: "we include a "_is_human" property to an agent. If it is set to "True", the (agent._act()) will opt to provide observations and memory information to a human user and wait for the human user to input the action."
  where: p.5, Sec 3.1
- Deployment claim: it serves agents as APIs with FastAPI, where other frameworks run in a terminal or Gradio. It also has an "Agent Hub" for sharing configs. The Hub is the config-as-data idea, like the declarative-JSON defence the note credits to Dibia et al. Tool calls use OpenAI function calling.
  number: none
  quote: "AGENTS supports deploying language agents as APIs with FastAPI"
  where: p.7, Sec 3.5-3.6
- Automatic SOP generation is a RAG-based "meta agent" that is itself built on AGENTS. It first specifies the agents, then plans the states, then generates the Components. The details are deferred to an unpublished paper.
  number: none
  quote: "Detailed description of the automatic agent creation framework is decribed in [Zhou et al., 2023b]." (ref: "Towards language agents uniting connectionism and symbolism. 2023b. To be published.")
  where: p.7 and p.10

LIMITS
- There is no quantitative evaluation of any kind: no benchmark, no user study, no comparison against LangChain or others on any metric. The claims "user-friendly", "non-specialists ... without much coding", "more stable/predictable" and "reduces the effort" are all unsupported by data.
- The authors do not list limitations. The only caveats are "Work in progress" and "ongoing effort".
- Table 1 is self-scored, with no versions given. Only the 2023 state of each framework is represented. Frameworks the note covers (LangGraph, ADK, Pydantic AI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework) are absent, and several of the compared ones have since changed. The note should treat it as a dated snapshot.
- The authors are the framework's own vendor (AIWaves), so there is a conflict of interest, similar to the Furgale caveat in the note.
- It does not discuss termination, loop limits, cost, failure modes, versioning, observability, evaluation or durability. It therefore cannot support or contradict the note's cost, stop-condition or lock-in measurements.
- "Towards AGI" is stated as a belief, not a result.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Franklin and Graesser, 1996, the agent-in-environment definition, which gives the Agent and Environment classes.
- Zhou et al. 2023a (RecurrentGPT), the memory components.
- Patil et al. 2023 (Gorilla), tool usage.
- Lewis et al. 2020 (RAG), automatic SOP generation.
- Reimers and Gurevych 2019 (Sentence-BERT).
- Nye et al. 2022 (scratchpads), task decomposition.
- Nakano et al. 2021 (WebGPT), web navigation.
- Schick et al. 2023 (Toolformer), tool use.
- Foerster et al. 2016, multi-agent communication.
- Park et al. 2023 (Generative Agents), Qian et al. 2023 and MetaGPT (Hong et al. 2023), multi-agent applications.
- Compared against: AutoGPT, BabyAGI, SuperAGI, Transformers Agents (Wolf et al. 2020), LangChain, Camel (Li et al. 2023), AgentVerse (Chen et al. 2023), Gentopia (Xu et al. 2023) and XLang.
- Also cited: Weng 2023 and Gur et al. 2023 (WebAgent).

CODE (verbatim from the extraction, p.4)
Code 1 (spacing garbled in the extraction):
  agents = Agent.from_config("./config.json"); sop = SOP.from_config("./config.json"); environment = Environment.from_config("./config.json"); run(agents, sop, environment)
Code 2:
  while not sop.finished:
      agent, state = sop.step(agents, environment)
      action = agent.step(state, environment)
      environment.update(agent, action)
  (optional dynamic planning: new_states = get_new_states(action); sop.add_states(new_states))
Note that the loop has no turn or call limit. `while not sop.finished` depends only on the SOP, so termination relies on the SOP or LLM transition function.

FIGURES (the figure-extraction script was not run, since the paper is a system description. Captions come from the text.)
- Fig 1, p.2: "Illustration of the AGENTS framework" (SOP, planning, web navigation, tool use, human-agent interaction, multi-agent communication). It gives the architecture overview.
- Fig 2, p.5: customer service agent screenshot. Fig 3, p.5: sales agent screenshot.
- Fig 4, p.6: multi-agent fiction studio. Fig 5, p.7: human-agent interaction in a debate.
- Figures 2-5 are UI screenshots and carry no data.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions were found.
- Code listing spacing is garbled by the extraction.
- Fig 2 and Fig 3 caption text is partly interleaved in the extraction.
- Suggested use for 06-framework-selection.md: at most a "sharpens" citation. It supports the design point that a state-graph SOP with LLM-driven transitions is an early example of explicit control flow versus model-chosen steps. It also supports declarative config as a lock-in defence. It gives no numbers the note can cite for cost, failure or adoption, and the Table 1 feature claims should be attributed as the authors' own.
